description: We are Chill Guys, united by our passion for STEM, technology, and space exploration. With skills in web development, design, problem-solving, and creativity, we work together to turn ideas into interactive experiences. For us, this challenge is not only about the final result. It is an opportunity to learn, collaborate, push our limits, and turn our curiosity about space into something we can share with others.
summary: Signal Delay is a free browser game that puts players in charge of a NASA-style robotic mission, from the drawing board to the last picture sent home. First they design it: pick a mission objective, choose a rocket and a science orbit, and pack instruments against four real limits shown live: weight, budget, power and data. Every choice is a trade-off. Then they fly it. Every order crosses space at the speed of light, using the real Earth–spacecraft distance on that mission day, so a solar storm can reach the spacecraft before the command does. At Mars, the robot asks what to observe; each picture costs fuel, battery or risk and must come home through a Deep Space Network pass. The Mission Report compares the flight with the real MAVEN mission and names one change to try next. Every number comes from physics or a cited NASA source, and real missions fly through the same model as the player. Solo, team, online or kids mode; no install, no account.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Communication Delays: Controlling a spacecraft millions of kilometres away is difficult because commands and replies take minutes to travel.

Mission Trade-offs: Every choice affects the mission. More equipment means more weight, power consumption and costs.

Missing Practical Experience: Learning about space missions through books and diagrams doesn't show what it feels like to plan and control one.

Complex Tools: Real mission-design tools are often too complicated for kids, students and beginners.

What exactly does the solution do

1. Design. Choose the goal (study the air, map the surface, or visit the moons), the rocket and the orbit, then pack parts into the rocket's nose. Four bars (weight, budget, power and data) move with every choice. The game will not launch until everything fits, and it says in plain words what is wrong and which part would fix it.

2. Fly. The clock runs day by day. When a danger appears (a solar storm, a dust storm, an eclipse, a fault), you choose a response, and your order travels at the speed of light across that day's real distance. In orbit, the robot asks what to photograph. Each picture costs fuel, battery or risk.

3. Learn. The Mission Report shows the real NASA pictures that came home, your stars, a comic of your flight, what saved you and what hurt you, and, at Mars, a comparison with NASA's real MAVEN mission. FLY AGAIN keeps your design, so you can change one thing and compare.

PROJECT OBJECTIVES

  • Create an interactive space mission design game based on real NASA data.
  • Help players understand communication delays between Earth and spacecraft.
  • Teach players how to design missions and manage resources.
  • Make space science accessible through simple, engaging gameplay.
  • Provide different learning experiences for kids, students and space enthusiasts.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Children (4–10): Space Kids, the same loop with big parts and no numbers, ending with real NASA facts.
  • Students: Cadet mode, the main game, with stars for the science brought home.
  • Classrooms: Team mode for up to four players (Flight Director, Engineer, Science Lead, Comms), who vote on each danger; each player can also join on their own phone with a room code. No accounts, no typed names, preset messages only, so it is safe for children.
  • Curious adults: Engineer mode shows the equation, the inputs and the source behind every number.
  • For everyone: free, in a browser, on a computer or a phone, in English and French.

How it is creative

Light delay is the game itself, not decoration: you watch your order crawl across space while the danger approaches. The robot talks back, late, like a real spacecraft, and its last message tells your flight as a story. The Daily mission is flown under the real Sun of the past week, using NASA's DONKI space-weather records.

Tools, coding languages and software

  • Core Engine & Physics: Custom physics engine written in TypeScript, responsible for all calculations and game logic.
  • Frontend & Visualization: React, Vite, Three.js (3D globes and visual displays).
  • Development & Testing: GitHub Actions, Vitest, Playwright, automated tests and real mission validation.
  • Infrastructure & Hosting: GitHub Pages (website hosting), GitHub Actions (automated deployment).
  • Online Multiplayer: Supabase (real-time relay for exchanging messages between players, without storing data).
  • Hardware Requirements: No special hardware required; compatible with any computer or phone with a web browser.
